title: Flipped voltage follower
description: The flipped voltage follower (FVF): a source follower whose bias current is held constant by a shunt feedback device, so the input device's gate-source voltage barely moves and the buffer is highly linear with very low output resistance. Because the current through the input device is fixed, its $V_{GS}$ is constant and the output tracks the input with little level-shift variation — the reason the FVF is the workhorse buffer inside low-dropout regulators and switched-capacitor drivers. The feedback device closes a local loop that multiplies the follower's already-low output resistance down to $R_{out} \approx g_{ds,in}/((g_{m,in} + g_{mb,in})*g_{m,fb})$, the body term entering because the output is the input device's source. This sheet sizes the DC operating point and low-frequency output resistance; the local loop's stability is a small-signal AC check the simulator owns. One current is typed, the bias source's $I_{in}$ into node X: the input device carries it down to the output, and the feedback device, the only other device on the output node, carries the same current on to ground. The branch's internal node is derived rather than declared: node X is the feedback device's gate, one gate-source voltage above its grounded source, and the input device's drain-source voltage is whatever remains of that above the output. Deriving it is also what makes the sheet state the cell's real output ceiling — see V_out. On the demo NMOS table both devices size against the same data.

params.name: V_out
params.note: output DC level (also the input follower's source node, and the feedback device's drain). Both walls on this level belong to the CELL rather than to the tool, and both MOVE with the inversion knobs and with the process. The floor is the feedback device's own saturation voltage — its drain-source voltage IS the output level, so the output cannot sit below it; a weaker inversion on that device drops the floor. The ceiling is node X minus the input device's saturation voltage — node X is the feedback device's gate-source voltage, so the ceiling tracks it upward. On the demo table at the shipped inversions that window is roughly 0.24 V to 0.37 V. Stated at this design point. Where the design is held fixed (a range end), the gate bias above this node is what stays put and the node is re-solved under it, between min and max.

params.name: I_in
params.note: the bias source's current into node X — the one current on this sheet that is typed. The input device carries it, held constant by the feedback, which is what linearizes the buffer; the feedback device carries the same current on to ground, since nothing else touches the output node

params.name: gm_id_fb
params.note: feedback device inversion: at the branch current I_in it sets gm_fb, hence the loop gain

doc.title: Shunt feedback device
doc.description: The feedback device that regulates the input device's current; its gm sets the loop gain that drives the output resistance down. It is the only other device on the output node, so it carries the input device's current, $I_{in}$, on to ground. Its source is at ground and its drain IS the output node, so its drain-source voltage is $V_{out}$ outright. Its gate is the branch's internal node X, and since that gate sits one gate-source voltage above the grounded source, sizing this device is what FIXES node X — there is nothing left about the node to type. It is placed first in the branch for exactly that reason: the input device's drain-source voltage is then measured down from the node this sizing produced.

doc.title: Input follower device
doc.description: The FVF input device. It carries the branch's fixed current, read from the feedback device below it in the same branch; its gm and output conductance set the base output resistance, and its constant current keeps its Vgs (hence the level shift) nearly fixed. Its source is the output node and its drain is node X, so its drain-source voltage is the distance between those two nodes rather than a free choice.

equations.name: V_x
equations.note: the branch's internal node — the input device's drain and the feedback device's gate. That gate sits one gate-source voltage above a grounded source, so the node is the feedback device's own sized gate-source voltage: derived, never typed

equations.name: gm_fb
equations.note: feedback device transconductance (the loop gain factor)

equations.name: Rout
equations.note: FVF output resistance: the follower output resistance divided down by the shunt-feedback loop gain gm_fb/gds_in. The source-body generator adds to gm because the output node is the input device's source while its body is at ground, the same form the super source follower uses

equations.name: Rout_plain
equations.note: the plain source-follower output resistance, for comparison

equations.name: headroom
equations.note: the stacked saturation voltage the FVF branch needs (input device over the feedback/current-source device)

equations.name: cgg_in
equations.note: estimate: the capacitance the input terminal presents, taken as the input device's whole gate capacitance. It OVERSTATES what a driver sees — the feedback holds this device's current, so its gate-source voltage barely moves and most of the gate-source capacitance is bootstrapped away. No check reads it

equations.name: I_q
equations.note: estimate: quiescent supply current — ONE stacked branch: the feedback device reuses the input device's current rather than drawing its own, so the supply pays for it once. A realization that biases the output node with a source of its own adds that current on top. The datasheet line for comparing designs; no check reads it

checks.note: the buffer output resistance meets the target
the supply must cover the output level plus the stacked saturation voltages of the FVF branch
